title: Acute & chronic leukaemias: cytogenetics, flow & smear
subject: Pathology
anchor: Bleeding + DIC + hypergranular blasts with bundles of Auer rods (faggot cells), CD34−/HLA-DR− → APL t(15;17) PML::RARA → start ATRA now
Child, bone pain, TdT+ CD19+ CD10+ blasts, MPO− → B-ALL; adolescent male + mediastinal mass + cCD3+ → T-ALL
Elderly, lymphocytosis, smudge cells, CD5+ CD23+ → CLL; massive spleen + dry tap + TRAP/CD103/CD11c/CD25 + BRAF V600E → hairy cell leukaemia
Very high WBC, full myeloid spectrum, basophilia, low LAP, splenomegaly → CML t(9;22) BCR::ABL1 p210
algorithm:
CBC + peripheral smear: cytopenias / leukocytosis / blasts
→ Blasts ≥20% (blood or marrow) = acute leukaemia (exam-classic cutoff)
  WHO-HAEM5: AML with defining genetic abnormality (e.g. PML::RARA, RUNX1::RUNX1T1, CBFB::MYH11) needs no blast cutoff | ICC 2022: ≥10%
→ Bone marrow aspirate + biopsy → flow cytometry for lineage
  MPO / Sudan black / CD13, CD33, CD117 → AML (Auer rods = myeloid)
  TdT + CD19, CD10, CD22, CD79a → B-ALL
  TdT + cytoplasmic CD3 (+CD7) → T-ALL
→ Karyotype / FISH / RT-PCR / NGS (FLT3, NPM1) → risk group
→ APL suspected on smear (DIC, faggot cells): give ATRA immediately, before genetic confirmation; ATRA + arsenic trioxide; support with platelets, FFP, cryoprecipitate
→ Mature-looking cells + high WBC:
  Lymphocytes, CD5+ CD23+ → CLL (B-lymphocytes ≥5×10⁹/L, clonal)
  Myeloid spectrum + basophilia → BCR::ABL1 → CML → imatinib (TKI)
  Leukemoid: LAP high, no basophilia, BCR::ABL1 negative

points: **Auer rods** = fused azurophilic (MPO+) granules → myeloid lineage; never in ALL
Monocytic AML (M4/M5): gum hypertrophy, skin infiltration (leukaemia cutis), CNS involvement, non-specific esterase positive
Down syndrome: acute megakaryoblastic leukaemia (M7) before age 5 (GATA1 mutation; transient abnormal myelopoiesis in newborns) and ↑ ALL risk
AML prognosis: NPM1 mutation without FLT3-ITD = favourable; FLT3-ITD, complex karyotype, TP53 = adverse
Leukostasis (very high blast count, usually AML): dyspnoea, hypoxia, confusion → cytoreduction/leukapheresis, avoid RBC transfusion before WBC falls

**Differentiation syndrome** with ATRA/ATO (days to ~3 weeks): fever, dyspnoea, pulmonary infiltrates, effusions, weight gain, hypotension, renal failure → dexamethasone 10 mg IV twice daily at first suspicion; interrupt ATRA/ATO only if severe
CML: imatinib inhibits BCR::ABL1 ATP-binding site; T315I mutation resistant to imatinib, dasatinib, nilotinib → ponatinib or asciminib
CLL staging: Rai (0–IV) and Binet (A–C); anaemia/thrombocytopenia = advanced stage
Tumour lysis syndrome (↑K, ↑PO₄, ↑uric acid, ↓Ca) → hydration + allopurinol, rasburicase if high risk (contraindicated in G6PD deficiency)

traps.stem: Young woman with gum bleeding, low fibrinogen, raised D-dimer; marrow full of granular blasts with Auer rods. Flow: CD13+, CD33+, MPO bright, CD34−, HLA-DR−.
traps.trap: Rejecting acute leukaemia because the 'blast markers' CD34 and HLA-DR are negative.
traps.fix: Classic APL is CD34− and HLA-DR−. Hypergranular cells + DIC + CD34−/HLA-DR− = APL; start ATRA immediately, do not wait for PML::RARA.

traps.stem: Elderly man with lymphocytosis; small B cells are CD5+. Which result separates CLL from mantle cell lymphoma?
traps.trap: Calling every CD5+ small B-cell disorder CLL.
traps.fix: CLL: CD23+, CD200+, cyclin D1−. Mantle cell lymphoma: CD23−, cyclin D1+ from t(11;14) CCND1::IGH, SOX11+.

traps.stem: WBC 70,000/µL with left shift in a patient with severe sepsis. CML or leukemoid reaction?
traps.trap: Choosing CML because of the very high count and myelocytes on the smear.
traps.fix: Leukemoid reaction: LAP high, toxic granulation/Döhle bodies, no basophilia, BCR::ABL1 negative. CML: LAP low, absolute basophilia, splenomegaly, Philadelphia chromosome/BCR::ABL1 positive.

cards.text: APL: translocation {{c1::t(15;17)}} forms {{c2::PML::RARA}}; classic flow is CD34 {{c3::negative}} and HLA-DR negative; start {{c4::ATRA}} before genetic confirmation.

cards.front: CLL vs mantle cell lymphoma: both CD5+ B cells. Two discriminating markers?
cards.back:
CLL: CD23+, cyclin D1−.
Mantle cell: CD23−, cyclin D1+ (t(11;14)), SOX11+.

cards.front: Three tests that confirm CML over a leukemoid reaction
cards.back:
1. LAP score low (high in leukemoid)
2. Absolute basophilia
3. Philadelphia chromosome / BCR::ABL1 on karyotype, FISH or RT-PCR

cards.text: Hairy cell leukaemia: driver mutation {{c1::BRAF V600E}}; most specific marker {{c2::annexin A1}}; marrow gives a {{c3::dry tap}}; drug of choice {{c4::cladribine}}.
BCR::ABL1 protein in CML is {{c1::p210}}; in most Ph+ ALL it is {{c2::p190 (p185)}}.

cards.front: Fever, dyspnoea, pulmonary infiltrates and weight gain 10 days after starting ATRA for APL: diagnosis and first step?
cards.back: Differentiation syndrome → dexamethasone 10 mg IV twice daily immediately; hold ATRA/ATO only if severe.

cards.front: Discriminator: AML vs ALL — deciding stain/marker?
cards.back: AML: Auer rods, myeloperoxidase+, CD13/33. ALL: TdT+, PAS+ (blocks), MPO−, CD10/19; children.

cards.front: Discriminator: CML vs leukaemoid reaction — deciding feature?
cards.back: CML: ↓LAP score, t(9;22), basophilia. Leukaemoid: ↑LAP, toxic granulation.

title: Hodgkin, NHL translocations & plasma cell neoplasms
subject: Pathology
anchor: Young adult, painless cervical/mediastinal nodes, alcohol-induced node pain, owl-eye cell CD15+ CD30+ CD45− → classic Hodgkin lymphoma
Jaw mass in African child, starry sky, Ki-67 ~100%, t(8;14) MYC → Burkitt lymphoma
Elderly, bone pain, hypercalcaemia, renal failure, anaemia, rouleaux, punched-out lytic lesions, M-spike → multiple myeloma
IgM spike + hyperviscosity (blurred vision, bleeding) + no lytic lesions + MYD88 L265P → Waldenström macroglobulinaemia

points: **Reed–Sternberg cell**: large, bilobed 'owl-eye' nuclei with prominent eosinophilic nucleoli; classic HL is CD15+, CD30+, PAX5 weak+, CD45−, usually CD20−; RS cells are of germinal-centre B-cell origin
Ann Arbor/Lugano: I = one node region; II = ≥2 regions same side of diaphragm; III = both sides; IV = diffuse extranodal (e.g. marrow, liver). Lugano 2014 uses PET-CT; A/B suffix retained only for HL
B symptoms: fever >38 °C, drenching night sweats, weight loss >10% in 6 months; pruritus and alcohol-induced pain are not B symptoms

Myeloma (IMWG 2014): clonal marrow plasma cells ≥10% or biopsy-proven plasmacytoma + ≥1 myeloma-defining event: **CRAB** (Ca >11 mg/dL, creatinine >2 mg/dL or CrCl <40 mL/min, Hb <10 g/dL, ≥1 lytic lesion) or **SLiM** (≥60% plasma cells, involved/uninvolved free light-chain ratio ≥100, >1 focal MRI lesion ≥5 mm)

**MGUS**: serum M-protein <3 g/dL, clonal plasma cells <10%, no CRAB/amyloidosis; progresses ~1% per year. Smouldering myeloma: M-protein ≥3 g/dL (or urine ≥500 mg/24 h) and/or plasma cells 10–59%, no myeloma-defining event
Myeloma lab clues: rouleaux, very high ESR, low anion gap (IgG), normal ALP, bone scan often negative (lytic lesions without osteoblastic activity) → whole-body low-dose CT/MRI/PET
M-protein frequency: IgG > IgA > light chain only; **Bence Jones protein** = free light chains in urine, missed by dipstick (detect by urine electrophoresis/immunofixation)
Plasma cell inclusions: **Russell bodies** (cytoplasmic Ig globules), Dutcher bodies (Ig invaginating into nucleus), Mott cells (grape cells), flame cells (IgA); markers CD138, CD38
Myeloma kidney: light-chain cast nephropathy (casts with Tamm–Horsfall protein); also AL amyloid, hypercalcaemia, Fanconi syndrome; infections are the commonest cause of death
Waldenström: IgM, lymphadenopathy and splenomegaly, hyperviscosity → plasmapheresis; lytic bone lesions are not a feature

traps.stem: Lymph node with scattered large 'popcorn' cells that are CD20+, CD45+, CD15−, CD30−.
traps.trap: Calling it classic Hodgkin lymphoma because large atypical cells sit in a lymphocyte-rich background.
traps.fix: This is nodular lymphocyte-predominant HL: LP (popcorn) cells keep B-cell markers (CD20+) and lack CD15/CD30. Classic RS cells are CD15+, CD30+, CD20−, CD45−.

traps.stem: Elderly man, hypercalcaemia, raised creatinine and back pain. Urine dipstick protein negative, but 24 h urine protein is high.
traps.trap: Excluding paraproteinaemia because the dipstick is negative.
traps.fix: Dipstick detects albumin, not free light chains. Bence Jones proteinuria needs urine protein electrophoresis/immunofixation; serum free light-chain assay is also used.

traps.stem: IgG M-protein 1.5 g/dL, marrow plasma cells 6%, normal calcium, creatinine and Hb, no bone lesions.
traps.trap: Labelling it multiple myeloma and starting chemotherapy.
traps.fix: MGUS: <3 g/dL M-protein, <10% plasma cells and no myeloma-defining event → observe; risk of progression ~1%/year.

cards.text: Classic Reed–Sternberg cells are {{c1::CD15}}+ and {{c2::CD30}}+, but CD45 negative; the lacunar cell is typical of {{c3::nodular sclerosis}} HL.

cards.front: Match the translocation: Burkitt, follicular, mantle cell, MALT, ALK+ ALCL
cards.back:
Burkitt t(8;14) MYC
Follicular t(14;18) BCL2
Mantle t(11;14) cyclin D1
MALT t(11;18) API2::MALT1
ALCL t(2;5) NPM1::ALK

cards.text: Myeloma-defining SLiM criteria: clonal plasma cells ≥{{c1::60%}}, involved/uninvolved free light-chain ratio ≥{{c2::100}}, and >1 focal MRI lesion ≥{{c3::5 mm}}.

cards.front: Why can a bone scan be normal in multiple myeloma?
cards.back: Lesions are purely lytic (osteoclast activation, osteoblast suppression), so there is little tracer uptake; use low-dose whole-body CT, MRI or PET-CT.

cards.text: Waldenström macroglobulinaemia: {{c1::IgM}} paraprotein, hyperviscosity, and the {{c2::MYD88 L265P}} mutation.

cards.front: Discriminator: Hodgkin vs non-Hodgkin lymphoma — deciding feature?
cards.back: Hodgkin: Reed-Sternberg cells (CD15+, CD30+), contiguous spread, cervical nodes, B symptoms. NHL: noncontiguous spread, extranodal involvement.

title: Haemolytic anaemias & peripheral smear clues
subject: Pathology
anchor: Anaemia + jaundice + splenomegaly + ↑MCHC + spherocytes + DAT negative + family history → hereditary spherocytosis
Haemolysis after fava beans, primaquine, dapsone or infection in a male; bite cells, Heinz bodies → G6PD deficiency
Haemolysis + pancytopenia + thrombosis at unusual sites (Budd–Chiari) + dark morning urine → PNH (CD55/CD59 loss)
Microcytosis with RBC count high, Mentzer index <13, HbA2 >3.5% → β-thalassaemia trait
algorithm:
Anaemia + ↑reticulocytes, ↑unconjugated bilirubin, ↑LDH, ↓haptoglobin = haemolysis
→ Peripheral smear + direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test
  DAT positive → immune haemolysis
    IgG, warm (37 °C), spherocytes, extravascular (spleen) → warm AIHA (SLE, CLL, methyldopa)
    C3d only, IgM, cold → cold agglutinin disease (Mycoplasma, EBV, lymphoma)
  DAT negative → look at the smear
    Spherocytes → EMA binding (flow) / osmotic fragility → hereditary spherocytosis
    Bite cells, Heinz bodies → G6PD assay (repeat 2–3 months after crisis)
    Schistocytes → MAHA: check platelets, PT/aPTT, ADAMTS13, creatinine (TTP/HUS/DIC)
    Sickle/target cells → Hb electrophoresis / HPLC
    No clue + intravascular haemolysis + cytopenia → flow cytometry for CD55/CD59 (FLAER) → PNH

points: **Intravascular** haemolysis: haemoglobinaemia, haemoglobinuria, haemosiderinuria, very low haptoglobin (PNH, G6PD crisis, ABO mismatch, MAHA, PCH). **Extravascular**: splenomegaly, spherocytes (HS, warm AIHA)
HS: aplastic crisis with parvovirus B19; pigment gallstones; splenectomy cures anaemia (delay to >6 years; vaccinate against encapsulated organisms)
G6PD triggers: primaquine, dapsone, sulfonamides, nitrofurantoin, rasburicase, methylene blue, fava beans, infection; Mediterranean variant more severe than African A−
Sickle cell: autosplenectomy (Howell–Jolly bodies), Salmonella osteomyelitis, dactylitis in infants, acute chest syndrome; hydroxyurea raises HbF
**Mentzer index** = MCV ÷ RBC count (millions/µL): <13 suggests thalassaemia trait, >13 iron deficiency
α-thalassaemia: 3 genes deleted = HbH disease (β₄); 4 deleted = Hb Bart's (γ₄) → hydrops fetalis
β-thalassaemia major: hair-on-end skull X-ray, chipmunk facies, extramedullary haematopoiesis, iron overload → chelation
PNH: thrombosis (hepatic, portal, cerebral veins) is the leading cause of death; associated with aplastic anaemia; treated with complement C5 inhibitor eculizumab
Haemolysis drives reticulocytosis → MCV may be mildly ↑; folate demand ↑ (give folic acid)

traps.stem: Black male develops haemolysis on day 2 of primaquine. G6PD level measured on day 4 is normal.
traps.trap: Excluding G6PD deficiency on the normal assay.
traps.fix: Old enzyme-deficient RBCs have already lysed; young reticulocytes have more G6PD → falsely normal. Repeat the assay 2–3 months after the episode.

traps.stem: Microcytic anaemia, Hb 10.5 g/dL, MCV 64 fL, RBC 6.0 million/µL, ferritin normal.
traps.trap: Diagnosing iron deficiency from microcytosis alone and prescribing iron.
traps.fix: Mentzer index 64/6 ≈ 10.7 (<13) → β-thalassaemia trait; confirm with HbA2 >3.5% on HPLC/electrophoresis. Note coexistent iron deficiency can lower HbA2.

traps.stem: Spherocytes on smear in a patient with anaemia and splenomegaly. Which test separates the two common causes?
traps.trap: Using osmotic fragility to diagnose hereditary spherocytosis.
traps.fix: Spherocytes from any cause (including warm AIHA) have ↑ osmotic fragility. Do the DAT first: positive = AIHA; negative + family history + reduced EMA binding = HS.

cards.text: PNH: acquired {{c1::PIGA}} mutation → loss of GPI-anchored {{c2::CD55 and CD59}}; screening test of choice is {{c3::flow cytometry (FLAER)}}.
β-thalassaemia trait: HbA2 {{c1::>3.5%}} and Mentzer index {{c2::<13}}.

cards.front: Warm vs cold AIHA: antibody class, temperature, complement, and classic causes
cards.back:
Warm: IgG, 37 °C, extravascular, spherocytes; SLE, CLL, methyldopa.
Cold: IgM, <37 °C, complement C3d, agglutination; Mycoplasma, EBV, lymphoma.

cards.front: Most commonly affected protein in hereditary spherocytosis, and the preferred screening test?
cards.back: Ankyrin; eosin-5′-maleimide (EMA) binding test by flow cytometry (reduced fluorescence).

cards.text: Howell–Jolly bodies indicate {{c1::asplenia/hyposplenism}}; basophilic stippling suggests {{c2::lead poisoning}} or thalassaemia.

cards.front: Discriminator: Intravascular vs extravascular haemolysis — deciding feature?
cards.back: Intravascular: haemoglobinuria, ↓haptoglobin, haemosiderinuria (PNH, G6PD crisis, MAHA). Extravascular: splenomegaly, spherocytes (hereditary spherocytosis, warm AIHA).

cards.front: Discriminator: Warm vs cold AIHA — deciding feature?
cards.back: Warm: IgG, 37 °C, spleen, steroids; (SLE, CLL). Cold: IgM + complement, C3 on Coombs, <30 °C, Mycoplasma/EBV, agglutination, avoid cold.

Schistocytes (fragmented RBCs, helmet cells) = MAHA, e.g. TTP
Sickle cell anaemia: sickle cells with target cells and polychromasia

title: Bleeding & clotting disorders: PT/aPTT/BT logic
subject: Pathology
anchor: Mucocutaneous bleeding (petechiae, epistaxis, menorrhagia) = platelet/vWF problem; deep bleeds (haemarthrosis, muscle haematoma) = coagulation factor problem
Fever + MAHA (schistocytes) + thrombocytopenia + neuro signs + renal involvement, normal PT/aPTT → TTP (ADAMTS13 <10%)
Child after bloody diarrhoea + MAHA + thrombocytopenia + AKI → HUS (Shiga toxin E. coli O157:H7)
Platelet fall >50% 5–10 days after heparin ± new thrombosis → HIT
algorithm:
Bleeding patient: platelet count, PT/INR, aPTT, fibrinogen, smear
→ Low platelets only
  Isolated, well patient, normal smear → ITP (diagnosis of exclusion)
  Schistocytes → TTP / HUS (PT/aPTT normal) vs DIC (PT/aPTT ↑, fibrinogen ↓, D-dimer ↑)
→ Normal platelets, isolated ↑aPTT
  Mixing study (1:1 with normal plasma)
    Corrects → factor deficiency (VIII, IX, XI, XII) or vWD
    Does not correct → inhibitor: lupus anticoagulant (thrombosis, not bleeding) or acquired factor VIII inhibitor (prolongs further on incubation)
→ Isolated ↑PT → factor VII deficiency, early vitamin K deficiency, early liver disease, warfarin
→ PT and aPTT both ↑ → common pathway (X, V, II, fibrinogen), vitamin K deficiency, liver disease, DIC
→ All normal but bleeding → vWD, platelet function defect (aspirin, Glanzmann, Bernard–Soulier), factor XIII deficiency, scurvy, vascular

points: **vWD** is the most common inherited bleeding disorder; type 1 (partial quantitative, AD) is commonest; DDAVP releases stored vWF (avoid in type 2B: worsens thrombocytopenia)

TTP classic pentad: fever, MAHA, thrombocytopenia, neurological signs, renal dysfunction (full pentad uncommon). Treat urgently with plasma exchange ± steroids, caplacizumab; platelet transfusion generally avoided
Haemophilia A (VIII) is commoner than B (IX, Christmas disease); both X-linked recessive; carrier females usually asymptomatic

**HIT** (type II): IgG against heparin–PF4 complex → platelet activation → thrombosis more than bleeding. 4Ts score: Thrombocytopenia, Timing (5–10 days), Thrombosis, oTher cause absent. Stop all heparin, start non-heparin anticoagulant (argatroban, bivalirudin, fondaparinux, DOAC); avoid platelet transfusion; no warfarin until platelets recover
**Factor V Leiden** (Arg506Gln, activated protein C resistance) is the most common inherited thrombophilia in Caucasians; prothrombin G20210A second
Antithrombin deficiency → heparin resistance; protein C deficiency → warfarin-induced skin necrosis (start warfarin with heparin bridge)
Antiphospholipid syndrome: lupus anticoagulant prolongs aPTT in vitro but causes arterial/venous thrombosis and recurrent pregnancy loss
Newborn vitamin K deficiency (haemorrhagic disease of the newborn) → prophylactic IM vitamin K at birth
Factor XIII deficiency: normal PT, aPTT, platelets; delayed bleeding and umbilical stump bleeding → urea clot solubility test

traps.stem: Patient with prolonged aPTT that fails to correct on mixing; has had two DVTs and a miscarriage.
traps.trap: Assuming a bleeding disorder because the aPTT is prolonged.
traps.fix: Non-correcting aPTT = inhibitor. With thrombosis and pregnancy loss this is lupus anticoagulant (antiphospholipid syndrome), a prothrombotic state.

traps.stem: Fever, confusion, Hb 7 g/dL with schistocytes, platelets 15,000/µL, PT and aPTT normal. Platelet transfusion requested.
traps.trap: Treating as DIC or transfusing platelets.
traps.fix: Normal PT/aPTT with MAHA and thrombocytopenia = TTP. Start plasma exchange urgently; platelets may worsen microthrombosis. DIC would show ↑PT/aPTT and ↓fibrinogen.

traps.stem: Platelet disorder with large platelets and absent ristocetin-induced agglutination, versus one with normal count and absent aggregation to ADP.
traps.trap: Mixing up the glycoproteins.
traps.fix: Bernard–Soulier = GPIb (binds vWF), giant platelets, low count, ristocetin abnormal. Glanzmann = GPIIb/IIIa (binds fibrinogen), normal count/size, ristocetin normal.

cards.text: TTP is due to deficiency of {{c1::ADAMTS13}}, the protease that cleaves {{c2::ultra-large von Willebrand factor multimers}}; first-line treatment is {{c3::plasma exchange}}.

cards.front: Isolated prolonged aPTT, normal platelets: what does a mixing study tell you?
cards.back:
Corrects → factor deficiency (VIII, IX, XI, XII).
Does not correct → inhibitor (lupus anticoagulant or acquired factor VIII inhibitor).

cards.text: In vitamin K deficiency the {{c1::PT}} prolongs first because factor {{c2::VII}} has the shortest half-life.

cards.front: DIC vs liver disease: one factor that separates them
cards.back: Factor VIII: low in DIC (consumed), normal or raised in liver disease (made by endothelium/sinusoidal cells).

cards.text: The most common inherited bleeding disorder is {{c1::von Willebrand disease}}; the most common inherited thrombophilia is {{c2::factor V Leiden}}.

cards.front: HIT: timing, mechanism, and management
cards.back: Platelets fall >50% 5–10 days after heparin (sooner if recent exposure); IgG to heparin–PF4 → platelet activation and thrombosis. Stop all heparin, start argatroban/bivalirudin/fondaparinux/DOAC; no platelet transfusion; delay warfarin.

cards.front: Discriminator: TTP vs HUS — deciding feature?
cards.back: Both: MAHA + thrombocytopenia, normal PT/aPTT. TTP = ADAMTS13 <10% (neurological signs, fever, adults); HUS = Shiga-toxin/complement, renal failure dominant (children, bloody diarrhoea). Treat TTP with plasma exchange; typical HUS supportive.

cards.front: Discriminator: DIC vs TTP — deciding lab?
cards.back: DIC: prolonged PT/aPTT, ↓fibrinogen, ↑D-dimer. TTP: PT/aPTT normal.

cards.front: Discriminator: ITP vs TTP — deciding feature?
cards.back: ITP: isolated thrombocytopenia, no anaemia/schistocytes. TTP: schistocytes (MAHA) + organ dysfunction.

cards.front: Discriminator: Haemophilia A vs von Willebrand disease — deciding feature?
cards.back: Haemophilia A: X-linked, joint/muscle bleeds, prolonged aPTT, normal bleeding time. vWD: mucosal bleeding, prolonged bleeding time, ↓ristocetin aggregation, aPTT may be prolonged.

title: MPNs, MDS, aplastic anaemia & transfusion essentials
subject: Pathology
anchor: Plethora, itching after a hot bath, erythromelalgia, splenomegaly, high Hct, low EPO, JAK2 V617F → polycythaemia vera
Massive splenomegaly + teardrop cells + leukoerythroblastic smear + dry tap → primary myelofibrosis
Elderly woman, macrocytic anaemia, normal/high platelets, hypolobated micromegakaryocytes, isolated del(5q) → MDS with low blasts and 5q deletion (lenalidomide)
Pancytopenia + hypocellular fatty marrow + no splenomegaly → aplastic anaemia

tables.title: Myeloproliferative neoplasms
head: MPN
Driver mutations
Key findings
Treatment
rows: Hb >16.5 g/dL men / >16 g/dL women (or Hct >49%/48%), panmyelosis, low serum EPO, aquagenic pruritus, Budd–Chiari
Phlebotomy to Hct <45%, low-dose aspirin, hydroxyurea if high risk
Platelets ≥450×10⁹/L, large hyperlobulated (staghorn) megakaryocytes, erythromelalgia, thrombosis and bleeding (acquired vWD at very high counts)
Teardrop cells, leukoerythroblastic picture, dry tap, reticulin/collagen fibrosis, massive splenomegaly, extramedullary haematopoiesis
Ruxolitinib (JAK1/2 inhibitor); allogeneic HSCT is the only cure
Neutrophilia with myelocyte peak, basophilia, low LAP; blast phase ≥20% blasts

points: Secondary polycythaemia (hypoxia, EPO-secreting RCC, HCC, cerebellar haemangioblastoma, uterine fibroid) has **high EPO**; PV has low EPO
WHO-HAEM5 drops the CML accelerated phase (chronic → blast phase); ICC 2022 retains it

**MDS**: cytopenia(s) + dysplasia in ≥10% of a lineage, blasts <20%; ring sideroblasts ≥15% (≥5% if SF3B1 mutated); pseudo-Pelger–Huët neutrophils, micromegakaryocytes; risk of AML; therapy-related after alkylators/topoisomerase II inhibitors

**Aplastic anaemia**: marrow cellularity <25%; severe = 2 of ANC <500/µL, platelets <20,000/µL, reticulocytes <20,000/µL (very severe if ANC <200). Causes: idiopathic (immune), drugs (chloramphenicol, gold, carbamazepine), benzene, seronegative hepatitis, PNH clone; inherited: Fanconi anaemia
Aplastic anaemia treatment: young + matched sibling → HSCT; others → horse ATG + cyclosporine + eltrombopag
**Bombay phenotype** (hh): no H antigen, serum has anti-A, anti-B and anti-H → can receive only Bombay blood (cross-matches incompatible with group O)
Universal donor: O Rh-negative packed RBCs; AB plasma is the universal plasma donor. Duffy-negative (Fy a−b−) RBCs resist P. vivax

Transfusion reactions: febrile non-haemolytic most common (prevent with leukoreduction); acute haemolytic = ABO mismatch (clerical error); anaphylaxis = IgA-deficient recipient with anti-IgA; TRALI within 6 h (donor anti-HLA/HNA antibodies, non-cardiogenic oedema, normal BNP); TACO = volume overload (hypertension, raised BNP); delayed haemolytic (often Kidd) at 3–10 days; TA-GVHD prevented only by irradiation
Storage: RBC 2–6 °C (CPDA-1 35 days; SAGM 42 days); platelets 20–24 °C with agitation, 5 days (highest bacterial contamination risk); cryoprecipitate contains fibrinogen, VIII, vWF, XIII

traps.stem: Smoker with Hct 56%, splenomegaly absent, raised serum EPO.
traps.trap: Diagnosing polycythaemia vera because the haematocrit is high.
traps.fix: Raised EPO = secondary polycythaemia (hypoxia, smoking/carboxyhaemoglobin, EPO-secreting tumour). PV has suppressed EPO and a JAK2 mutation.

traps.stem: Pancytopenia with splenomegaly and a dry tap on aspiration.
traps.trap: Calling it aplastic anaemia because the aspirate is empty.
traps.fix: Aplastic anaemia has no splenomegaly and a hypocellular fatty biopsy. Dry tap + splenomegaly suggests myelofibrosis, hairy cell leukaemia or marrow infiltration; do a trephine biopsy.

traps.stem: Acute respiratory distress 2 h after FFP transfusion; BP normal, BNP normal, bilateral infiltrates.
traps.trap: Labelling it TACO and giving diuretics.
traps.fix: TRALI: within 6 h, non-cardiogenic oedema, normal BNP, often hypotension; caused by donor anti-HLA/HNA antibodies (multiparous female plasma). Stop transfusion, supportive care. TACO has hypertension and high BNP.

cards.text: Polycythaemia vera: {{c1::JAK2 V617F}} mutation with {{c2::low}} serum erythropoietin; phlebotomy target haematocrit {{c3::<45%}}.

cards.front: Primary myelofibrosis: three classic findings
cards.back: Teardrop cells with leukoerythroblastic smear, dry tap with marrow fibrosis, massive splenomegaly (extramedullary haematopoiesis).

cards.text: The most common transfusion reaction is {{c1::febrile non-haemolytic}}; anaphylaxis occurs in {{c2::IgA-deficient}} recipients; TA-GVHD is prevented by {{c3::irradiation}}.

cards.front: Bombay blood group: what is missing and who can donate?
cards.back: H antigen absent (hh), so A/B cannot form; serum has anti-H. Only another Bombay phenotype donor is compatible.

cards.text: MDS with isolated del(5q): elderly women, macrocytic anaemia, normal or raised {{c1::platelets}}, responds to {{c2::lenalidomide}}.

title: Cell injury, necrosis, apoptosis & calcification
subject: Pathology
anchor: Cellular swelling is the earliest reversible change; amorphous mitochondrial densities and membrane rupture mark the point of no return
Single cells shrink, chromatin condenses, apoptotic bodies, no inflammation, DNA ladder → apoptosis
Intrinsic = mitochondria, BAX/BAK, cytochrome c, APAF-1, caspase-9; extrinsic = Fas/TNFR1, FADD, caspase-8; both converge on caspase-3
Annexin V+/PI− = early apoptosis; Annexin V+/PI+ = late apoptosis/necrosis

tables.title: Types of necrosis
head: Type
Mechanism / look
Classic example
rows: Protein denaturation; cell outlines (ghost cells) preserved for days
Ischaemic infarct of heart, kidney, spleen (any solid organ except brain)
Cheese-like, amorphous granular debris, architecture lost, within granuloma
Lipase releases fatty acids → calcium soaps (saponification, chalky white)
Immune complex + fibrin in vessel wall, bright pink
Dry = coagulative; wet = superadded bacterial liquefaction

tables.title: Apoptosis vs necrosis
head: Feature
Apoptosis
Necrosis
rows: Intact; phosphatidylserine flips outward (eat-me signal, binds annexin V)

points: Reversible injury: cellular (hydropic) swelling, fatty change, membrane blebs, ER dilation, myelin figures, loss of microvilli. Irreversible: **mitochondrial amorphous (flocculent) densities**, plasma/lysosomal membrane damage, nuclear dissolution

Intrinsic pathway: BH3-only sensors (BIM, BID, PUMA, NOXA, BAD) activate **BAX/BAK** → mitochondrial outer membrane permeabilisation → cytochrome c + APAF-1 = apoptosome → **caspase-9**. BCL-2, BCL-XL, MCL-1 are anti-apoptotic
Extrinsic pathway: FasL–Fas (CD95) or TNF–TNFR1 → FADD → **caspase-8**; FLIP blocks it; BID cleavage links extrinsic to intrinsic. Executioner caspases 3, 6, 7
Annexin V/PI flow quadrants: AnV−/PI− live; AnV+/PI− early apoptotic; AnV+/PI+ late apoptotic (secondary necrosis); AnV−/PI+ necrotic/damaged. TUNEL detects DNA fragmentation

Other death modes: **necroptosis** (RIPK1–RIPK3–MLKL, caspase-independent); **pyroptosis** (inflammasome → caspase-1, gasdermin D pores, IL-1β/IL-18 release); **ferroptosis** (iron-dependent lipid peroxidation, GPX4 failure)
**Autophagy**: self-digestion in nutrient deprivation; mTOR inhibition triggers it; markers LC3, beclin-1 (ATG6)
Free radicals: hydroxyl radical (•OH) most reactive; Fenton reaction (Fe²⁺ + H₂O₂); removed by SOD, catalase, glutathione peroxidase; antioxidant vitamins E, C, A

Accumulations: **lipofuscin** (wear-and-tear pigment, brown atrophy, heart/liver of elderly); **haemosiderin** (Prussian blue +); fatty change (Oil Red O/Sudan on frozen section); glycogen (PAS +, diastase-sensitive)

**Dystrophic calcification**: normal serum Ca, in dead/damaged tissue (atheroma, damaged valves, caseation, psammoma bodies). **Metastatic**: hypercalcaemia (hyperparathyroidism, vitamin D excess, bone destruction, renal failure), normal tissues that lose acid: lung alveolar walls, kidney, gastric mucosa, systemic arteries
Most hypoxia-sensitive cells: neurons (irreversible after ~3–5 min), then myocardium (~20–30 min); red neurons appear 12–24 h after ischaemia

traps.stem: Which morphological change best indicates irreversible ischaemic myocardial injury on electron microscopy?
traps.trap: Choosing cellular swelling or fatty change because they are the earliest visible changes.
traps.fix: Swelling and fatty change are reversible. Amorphous (flocculent) densities in mitochondria and plasma/lysosomal membrane rupture mark irreversibility.

traps.stem: Flow cytometry shows a population that binds annexin V but excludes propidium iodide.
traps.trap: Calling them necrotic because annexin V is positive.
traps.fix: Annexin V+/PI− = early apoptosis (membrane intact, phosphatidylserine exposed). PI entry (AnV+/PI+) means membrane breached → late apoptosis/necrosis.

traps.stem: Brain infarct a week old: which type of necrosis?
traps.trap: Coagulative necrosis, the rule for ischaemic infarcts.
traps.fix: The brain is the exception: ischaemic infarct of the CNS shows liquefactive necrosis (lipid-rich tissue, little stroma, microglial enzymes).

cards.text: Intrinsic apoptosis: {{c1::BAX/BAK}} release {{c2::cytochrome c}}, which with APAF-1 activates caspase-{{c3::9}}; extrinsic apoptosis activates caspase-{{c4::8}}.

cards.front: Annexin V / propidium iodide: what do the four quadrants mean?
cards.back:
AnV−/PI− live
AnV+/PI− early apoptosis
AnV+/PI+ late apoptosis / secondary necrosis
AnV−/PI+ necrosis

cards.text: Dystrophic calcification occurs with {{c1::normal}} serum calcium in damaged tissue; metastatic calcification needs {{c2::hypercalcaemia}} and favours {{c3::lung, kidney and gastric mucosa}}.

cards.front: Pyroptosis vs ferroptosis: key molecules
cards.back:
Pyroptosis: inflammasome → caspase-1 → gasdermin D pores, IL-1β/IL-18.
Ferroptosis: iron-dependent lipid peroxidation when GPX4/glutathione fails.

cards.text: Apoptotic DNA gives a {{c1::ladder}} pattern on gel electrophoresis; necrotic DNA gives a {{c2::smear}}.

title: Inflammation mediators, granulomas, healing & amyloid
subject: Pathology
anchor: Neutrophilia, recurrent infections without pus, delayed umbilical cord separation → leukocyte adhesion deficiency type 1 (CD18)
Epithelioid macrophages + Langhans giant cells ± central caseation → granuloma (TB caseating; sarcoid non-caseating)
Congo red: salmon-pink on light microscopy, apple-green birefringence under polarised light → amyloid (β-pleated sheet)
Collagen type III early in granulation tissue → replaced by type I during remodelling

tables.title: Mediators of acute inflammation
head: Action
Main mediators
rows: Histamine, prostaglandins (PGI₂, PGE₂, PGD₂), nitric oxide
Histamine (immediate transient, venules), bradykinin, C3a/C5a, LTC₄/D₄/E₄, PAF, substance P
C5a, LTB₄, IL-8 (CXCL8), bacterial N-formyl-methionyl peptides
IL-1, TNF, IL-6 → PGE₂ in hypothalamus
LTC₄, LTD₄, LTE₄ (slow-reacting substance of anaphylaxis)

tables.title: Amyloid types
head: Type
Precursor
Setting
rows: Plasma cell neoplasm / primary amyloidosis; heart, kidney, macroglossia, periorbital purpura
Chronic inflammation: RA, TB, bronchiectasis, osteomyelitis, IBD, familial Mediterranean fever; kidney first
Familial amyloid polyneuropathy; wild-type senile cardiac amyloidosis
Alzheimer plaques, cerebral amyloid angiopathy, Down syndrome
Type 2 diabetes islets / medullary thyroid carcinoma / isolated atrial amyloid

points: Leukocyte recruitment: margination → rolling (**selectins** E, P, L binding sialyl-Lewis X) → firm adhesion (**integrins** LFA-1/Mac-1 to ICAM-1; VLA-4 to VCAM-1) → transmigration (**PECAM-1/CD31**) → chemotaxis

**LAD-1**: β2-integrin (CD18) defect, delayed cord separation, no pus, marked neutrophilia. **LAD-2**: fucosylation defect → no sialyl-Lewis X, Bombay phenotype, intellectual disability. Chédiak–Higashi: LYST, giant granules, albinism, neuropathy

Granuloma drivers: macrophage IL-12 → Th1 IFN-γ → epithelioid macrophages; TNF maintains granulomas (anti-TNF reactivates TB). Langhans giant cell: nuclei in a horseshoe at the periphery; foreign-body giant cell: nuclei scattered
Non-caseating granulomas: sarcoidosis, Crohn disease, berylliosis, foreign body, leprosy (tuberculoid); stellate necrotising granulomas in cat-scratch disease and lymphogranuloma venereum

Healing: granulation tissue = new capillaries + fibroblasts + loose ECM (VEGF, FGF-2, TGF-β). Wound strength ~10% at 1 week, ~70–80% by 3 months, never 100%. Vitamin C needed for prolyl/lysyl hydroxylation
Keloid extends beyond the original wound margins (excess collagen; predisposition in darker skin); hypertrophic scar stays within margins

Amyloid: non-branching fibrils 7.5–10 nm on EM, β-pleated sheet; Congo red apple-green birefringence; abdominal fat pad aspirate or rectal biopsy for diagnosis. Kidney is the most commonly and most seriously involved organ (nephrotic syndrome). Sago spleen = follicular deposits; lardaceous spleen = red pulp/sinusoidal

**Russell bodies** = immunoglobulin in dilated ER of plasma cells. **Mallory–Denk bodies** = ubiquitinated keratin 8/18 intermediate filaments in hepatocytes (alcoholic hepatitis, NASH, Wilson disease)
Hyaline (glassy pink): intracellular (Mallory–Denk, Russell bodies, protein reabsorption droplets in tubules) vs extracellular (hyaline arteriolosclerosis, amyloid, hyaline membranes in ARDS)

traps.stem: Infant with omphalitis, umbilical cord still attached at 5 weeks, WBC 40,000/µL, infected sites without pus.
traps.trap: Choosing chronic granulomatous disease because of recurrent bacterial infections.
traps.fix: Delayed cord separation + neutrophilia + no pus = LAD-1 (CD18 integrin defect, neutrophils cannot leave vessels). CGD forms abscesses/granulomas with catalase-positive organisms.

traps.stem: Congo red stained renal biopsy shows red-orange deposits on ordinary light. What confirms amyloid?
traps.trap: Accepting the red colour alone as diagnostic.
traps.fix: Apple-green birefringence under polarised light is required; EM shows non-branching 7.5–10 nm fibrils. Typing (AL vs AA vs ATTR) needs immunohistochemistry or mass spectrometry.

traps.stem: Patient on long-term haemodialysis develops bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome.
traps.trap: AL amyloid because it is the most common systemic type.
traps.fix: Dialysis-related amyloid is Aβ2M (β2-microglobulin is not filtered by older dialysis membranes).

cards.text: Leukocyte rolling uses {{c1::selectins}}, firm adhesion uses {{c2::integrins}}, and transmigration uses {{c3::PECAM-1 (CD31)}}.
Amyloid on Congo red shows {{c1::apple-green birefringence}} under polarised light because of its {{c2::β-pleated sheet}} structure.

cards.front: AL vs AA amyloid: precursor and typical setting
cards.back:
AL: immunoglobulin light chain (λ > κ), plasma cell neoplasm.
AA: serum amyloid A from chronic inflammation (RA, TB, bronchiectasis, FMF).

cards.text: Early granulation tissue contains collagen type {{c1::III}}, which is replaced by type {{c2::I}} during remodelling.

cards.front: Most important chemotactic agents for neutrophils
cards.back: C5a, LTB₄, IL-8 (CXCL8), bacterial N-formyl-methionyl peptides.

title: Hypersensitivity, rejection, immunodeficiency & HLA
subject: Pathology
anchor: Boy >6 months, recurrent pyogenic infections, absent tonsils, no CD19+ B cells → Bruton X-linked agammaglobulinaemia (BTK)
Hypocalcaemic tetany + conotruncal heart defect + absent thymic shadow + cleft palate → DiGeorge (22q11.2 deletion)
Eczema + thrombocytopenia with small platelets + recurrent infections in a boy → Wiskott–Aldrich syndrome
Catalase-positive infections (S. aureus, Aspergillus, Serratia, Nocardia, Burkholderia) + abnormal NBT/DHR → chronic granulomatous disease

head: Type
Mechanism
Examples
rows: Anaphylaxis, allergic asthma, hay fever, urticaria, food allergy
IgG/IgM against cell-surface or matrix antigen → lysis, opsonisation or receptor dysfunction
AIHA, ITP, ABO transfusion reaction, haemolytic disease of newborn, Goodpasture, pemphigus vulgaris, acute rheumatic fever, myasthenia gravis and Graves (receptor antibodies), hyperacute rejection
Circulating antigen–antibody complexes deposit → complement + neutrophils
SLE, post-streptococcal GN, serum sickness, Arthus reaction, polyarteritis nodosa
CD4 Th1/Th17 cytokines or CD8 cytotoxicity (48–72 h)
Tuberculin test, contact dermatitis, granulomas, type 1 diabetes, multiple sclerosis, Hashimoto thyroiditis, acute cellular rejection, GVHD

head: Disorder
Defect
Discriminating features
rows: BTK; B cells fail to mature
Boys after 6 months (maternal IgG wanes); all Ig ↓; absent B cells, tonsils, nodes; enteroviral meningoencephalitis, Giardia
Thymic hypoplasia (T-cell ↓), hypoparathyroidism, conotruncal defects, facial dysmorphism
X-linked IL2RG (common γ chain) most common; ADA deficiency (AR)
Failure to thrive, candidiasis, PCP, absent thymic shadow; HSCT; no live vaccines
Eczema, thrombocytopenia with small platelets, infections; ↓IgM, ↑IgA and IgE
No respiratory burst; catalase-positive organisms; NBT stays colourless, DHR flow test abnormal (test of choice)
CD40L on T cells (X-linked) most common
No class switching: ↑ or normal IgM, ↓IgG/IgA/IgE; Pneumocystis, Cryptosporidium
Onset in adolescence/adulthood; low IgG with B cells present; autoimmunity, lymphoma, bronchiectasis
Most common PID; often asymptomatic; anaphylaxis to blood products (anti-IgA)
C1-INH / early (C1q, C2, C4) / C3 / terminal C5–C9
Hereditary angioedema (low C4) / SLE-like disease / severe pyogenic infections / recurrent Neisseria

tables.title: HLA associations
head: HLA
Association
rows: Ankylosing spondylitis, reactive arthritis, psoriatic and IBD arthritis, acute anterior uveitis
Type 1 diabetes, SLE, Graves, Addison, myasthenia gravis, dermatitis herpetiformis
Rheumatoid arthritis (shared epitope, DRB1*04), type 1 diabetes
Coeliac disease (DQ2 in ~90–95%); DQ8 also type 1 diabetes
Carbamazepine (and phenytoin) SJS/TEN in South/East Asians

points: HLA genes lie on chromosome **6p**; class I (A, B, C) present to CD8 T cells; class II (DP, DQ, DR) present to CD4 T cells
**Hyperacute rejection**: minutes to hours, preformed anti-donor (ABO/HLA) antibodies, type II, thrombosis and cyanotic graft; prevented by cross-match
**Acute rejection**: days–months; cellular (T-cell, tubulitis, endotheliitis) or antibody-mediated (C4d in peritubular capillaries); responds to immunosuppression
**Chronic rejection**: months–years; intimal fibrosis / obliterative arteriopathy, interstitial fibrosis; bronchiolitis obliterans in lung, vanishing bile ducts in liver; not reversible
**GVHD**: immunocompetent donor T cells attack an immunocompromised host; skin, liver (bile ducts), GI tract; seen after HSCT or unirradiated transfusion; prevented by irradiating blood products
Ataxia–telangiectasia: ATM gene, IgA deficiency, sinopulmonary infections, lymphoma risk, ↑AFP; Job (hyper-IgE) syndrome: STAT3, cold abscesses, eczema, retained primary teeth
Live vaccines are contraindicated in SCID and XLA (e.g. oral polio, BCG); in DiGeorge depends on T-cell count

traps.stem: Boy with recurrent sinopulmonary infections; low IgG and IgA with normal/high IgM; Pneumocystis pneumonia.
traps.trap: Choosing XLA or CVID because immunoglobulins are low.
traps.fix: High/normal IgM with low IgG/A/E = hyper-IgM syndrome (CD40L defect → no class switching). Opportunistic Pneumocystis reflects the T-cell help defect.

traps.stem: Graft kidney turns dusky and mottled on the table within minutes of reperfusion.
traps.trap: Acute cellular rejection (T-cell mediated).
traps.fix: Minutes = hyperacute rejection from preformed antibodies (type II hypersensitivity). Acute cellular rejection takes days to weeks.

traps.stem: Graves disease and myasthenia gravis: which hypersensitivity type?
traps.trap: Type IV because they are autoimmune diseases, or type III because antibodies are involved.
traps.fix: Type II (antibody against a cell-surface receptor): stimulating anti-TSH receptor in Graves, blocking anti-AChR in myasthenia.

cards.text: CGD: defect in {{c1::NADPH oxidase}}; NBT test stays {{c2::colourless (negative)}}; preferred test is {{c3::DHR flow cytometry}}.

cards.front: XLA vs CVID: discriminating features
cards.back:
XLA: boys, onset after 6 months, BTK defect, B cells absent, no tonsils/nodes.
CVID: either sex, later onset, B cells present but fail to differentiate; autoimmunity, lymphoma.

cards.text: Abacavir hypersensitivity is linked to HLA-{{c1::B*57:01}}; carbamazepine SJS/TEN to HLA-{{c2::B*15:02}}.
Wiskott–Aldrich triad: {{c1::eczema}}, {{c2::thrombocytopenia with small platelets}}, and recurrent infections.

cards.front: Antibody-mediated acute renal rejection: tissue marker?
cards.back: C4d deposition in peritubular capillaries.

cards.text: Recurrent Neisseria infections suggest deficiency of terminal complement {{c1::C5–C9 (MAC)}}; hereditary angioedema is {{c2::C1 esterase inhibitor}} deficiency.

verify: Robbins 10e ch 6; IUIS 2022 classification of inborn errors of immunity
algorithm:
Hypersensitivity: which type? Ask — antibody or T cell, how fast?
→ Minutes, IgE on mast cells → Type I (anaphylaxis, atopy, urticaria) → adrenaline IM 0.5 mg
→ Antibody against cell or tissue antigen (IgG / IgM)
  Cell-surface (transfusion reaction, haemolytic anaemia, ITP, Rh) → Type II
  Receptor stimulating / blocking (Graves, myasthenia gravis) → Type II
→ Immune-complex deposit (IgG + antigen) 1–2 weeks → Type III (serum sickness, SLE, PSGN, Arthus)
→ T cell mediated, 48–72 h → Type IV (tuberculin test, contact dermatitis, granuloma, graft rejection)
  Memory aid: ACID — Anaphylactic, Cytotoxic, Immune complex, Delayed

subject: Pathology
anchor: Proto-oncogene: one mutated allele is enough (gain of function); tumour suppressor: both alleles lost (Knudson two-hit)
Psammoma bodies (concentric laminated calcification) → papillary thyroid carcinoma, serous ovarian tumours, meningioma, mesothelioma
Undifferentiated tumour → IHC panel: cytokeratin (carcinoma), vimentin (sarcoma), CD45 (lymphoma), S-100/HMB-45 (melanoma)

points: IHC by lineage: **cytokeratin** epithelial; **vimentin** mesenchymal; **desmin** muscle (myogenin/MyoD1 for rhabdomyosarcoma); **S-100** melanoma, schwannoma, Langerhans cells; **HMB-45 / Melan-A / SOX10** melanoma; **chromogranin, synaptophysin** neuroendocrine; **CD45 (LCA)** lymphoid; **CD31, CD34, ERG** vascular; **GFAP** glial

Site/tumour IHC: CD117 (c-KIT) and DOG1 → GIST; CD99 (+NKX2.2) → Ewing sarcoma; TTF-1 → lung adenocarcinoma and thyroid; CDX2 → colorectal; PAX8 → kidney, thyroid, Müllerian; WT1 + calretinin → mesothelioma; CD1a/langerin → Langerhans cell histiocytosis
**Psammoma bodies**: papillary thyroid ca, papillary serous ovarian/endometrial tumours, meningioma, mesothelioma (also papillary RCC, prolactinoma); a form of dystrophic calcification

Carcinogens: aflatoxin B1 → HCC (TP53 codon 249); vinyl chloride → hepatic angiosarcoma; benzene → AML; asbestos → mesothelioma (but bronchogenic carcinoma is the commonest asbestos cancer); β-naphthylamine/aniline dyes → urothelial carcinoma; arsenic → skin SCC, lung, liver angiosarcoma; nickel/chromium → lung, nasal sinus; nitrosamines → gastric; alkylating agents → AML

Oncogenic infections: HPV16/18 (E6 → p53, E7 → RB), EBV (Burkitt, nasopharyngeal ca, Hodgkin), HBV/HCV (HCC), HTLV-1 (adult T-cell leukaemia), HHV-8 (Kaposi, primary effusion lymphoma), Merkel cell polyomavirus, H. pylori (gastric adenocarcinoma, MALT)

Paraneoplastic: small cell lung → SIADH, ectopic ACTH, Lambert–Eaton (anti-VGCC), anti-Hu; squamous lung → PTHrP hypercalcaemia; RCC → erythrocytosis (EPO), hypercalcaemia; thymoma → myasthenia, pure red cell aplasia; ovarian teratoma → anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis; pancreatic → Trousseau migratory thrombophlebitis; gastric → acanthosis nigricans, Leser–Trélat

**Hallmarks of cancer**: sustained proliferative signalling, evasion of growth suppressors, resisting cell death, replicative immortality (telomerase), angiogenesis, invasion and metastasis, reprogrammed metabolism (Warburg effect), immune evasion; enablers: genomic instability and tumour-promoting inflammation
Grading = degree of differentiation (histology); staging = spread (TNM) and has greater prognostic value
Most common route: carcinomas → lymphatics; sarcomas → blood. Exceptions: follicular thyroid, RCC, HCC, choriocarcinoma spread haematogenously

traps.stem: Undifferentiated tumour: cytokeratin −, CD45 −, vimentin +, S-100 +, HMB-45 +.
traps.trap: Calling it a sarcoma because only vimentin and S-100 are positive.
traps.fix: S-100 + HMB-45 (Melan-A) = melanoma, which is cytokeratin-negative and vimentin-positive. Schwannoma is S-100+ but HMB-45−.

traps.stem: Man with a testicular mass and markedly raised AFP; histology reported as pure seminoma.
traps.trap: Accepting pure seminoma and planning seminoma-only therapy.
traps.fix: Pure seminoma does not produce AFP. Raised AFP means a non-seminomatous component (yolk sac tumour) → manage as NSGCT.

traps.stem: Which gene is the most frequently mutated in human cancers, and which oncogene is most often mutated?
traps.trap: Choosing RB or MYC because they are the best-known examples.
traps.fix: TP53 is the most commonly mutated gene overall; RAS (KRAS) is the most commonly mutated oncogene.

traps.stem: Adult diffuse astrocytoma with no necrosis or microvascular proliferation, IDH-wildtype, TERT promoter mutation and EGFR amplification.
traps.trap: Grading it as a low-grade (grade 2) diffuse astrocytoma on histology.

traps.stem: Rosette type in retinoblastoma vs medulloblastoma.
traps.trap: Swapping Homer Wright and Flexner–Wintersteiner.
traps.fix: Flexner–Wintersteiner = true rosette with a lumen (retinoblastoma). Homer Wright = no lumen, fibrillary core (medulloblastoma, neuroblastoma).

traps.stem: Child with a 4th-ventricle tumour; histology shows tumour cells radially arranged around blood vessels with an anuclear fibrillary zone.
traps.trap: Medulloblastoma, because it is the common malignant posterior fossa tumour in children.
traps.fix: Perivascular pseudorosettes = ependymoma (from the floor of the 4th ventricle, can extend through foramina). Medulloblastoma shows Homer Wright rosettes and arises from the vermis/roof.

points: **Barrett oesophagus**: intestinal metaplasia with goblet cells in distal oesophagus (columnar mucosa) → oesophageal adenocarcinoma; squamous cell carcinoma is linked to smoking/alcohol, middle third

**Coeliac disease** (modified Marsh): 1 = ↑ intraepithelial lymphocytes (>25/100 enterocytes); 2 = + crypt hyperplasia; 3a/b/c = partial/subtotal/total villous atrophy. Biopsy distal duodenum; IgA anti-tTG screening (check total IgA)

Colonic polyps: hyperplastic (serrated, minimal risk); tubular adenoma commonest; villous adenoma has highest malignant potential (and can cause hypokalaemia); Peutz–Jeghers (STK11) and juvenile polyps are hamartomas

Lung: **asbestosis** = lower-lobe fibrosis, ferruginous (asbestos) bodies, pleural plaques (commonest lesion); silicosis = upper lobes, eggshell hilar calcification, ↑TB. **Small cell carcinoma**: central, smoker, salt-and-pepper chromatin, nuclear moulding, crush artefact, neuroendocrine markers. Liver: **Mallory–Denk bodies** (alcoholic hepatitis, NASH, Wilson); Councilman (acidophil) bodies = apoptotic hepatocytes in acute viral hepatitis; ground-glass hepatocytes = HBsAg in chronic HBV; HCV = lymphoid aggregates + steatosis
Hereditary haemochromatosis: HFE C282Y, Prussian blue-positive hepatocyte iron, 'bronze diabetes', cirrhosis, HCC; Wilson: ATP7B, rhodanine stain for copper

Breast: invasive ductal (NST) is the commonest carcinoma; invasive lobular = single-file cells, loss of **E-cadherin (CDH1)**, often bilateral/multicentric; Paget disease of nipple = underlying DCIS/carcinoma
**Hürthle (oncocytic) cells**: large cells with abundant granular eosinophilic cytoplasm packed with mitochondria; in Hashimoto thyroiditis and oncocytic thyroid neoplasms
Gastric: H. pylori → antral gastritis, adenocarcinoma, MALT lymphoma; signet-ring cells → diffuse-type gastric cancer (CDH1 in hereditary diffuse type), linitis plastica, Krukenberg tumour

subject: Pathology
anchor: Disease worsens / appears earlier in successive generations → anticipation → trinucleotide repeat expansion

Same 15q11–q13 deletion: paternal → Prader–Willi (hyperphagia, hypotonia); maternal → Angelman (happy puppet, seizures)
Developmental delay with normal karyotype → chromosomal microarray (first-tier test)

head: Test
Detects

rows: Aneuploidy, balanced and unbalanced translocations, large deletions (~5–10 Mb); needs dividing cells
Targeted known loci: microdeletions (22q11, Williams 7q11, PWS/AS 15q), rapid aneuploidy screen (13, 18, 21, X, Y), fusion genes (BCR::ABL1); works on interphase nuclei
Only the probe region; not genome-wide

points: **AD**: structural/receptor proteins, every generation, 50% risk, variable expressivity, incomplete penetrance, new mutations (achondroplasia with advanced paternal age). Examples: ADPKD, Marfan, NF1/NF2, FH, Huntington, hereditary spherocytosis
**AR**: enzyme defects, horizontal pattern, consanguinity, 25% risk: CF, sickle cell, thalassaemia, PKU, Wilson, haemochromatosis, most storage disorders

**X-linked recessive**: males affected, no male-to-male transmission: DMD/BMD, haemophilia A/B, G6PD, Fabry, Hunter, Lesch–Nyhan, Bruton, WAS, CGD (X-linked form). **X-linked dominant**: hypophosphataemic rickets, Rett syndrome (lethal in males), incontinentia pigmenti
**Mitochondrial**: maternal transmission only, heteroplasmy → variable severity; LHON, MELAS, MERRF (ragged-red fibres), Leigh; Kearns–Sayre (large deletion, usually sporadic)

**Imprinting** (15q11–q13): Prader–Willi = loss of paternal genes: paternal deletion (~70%), maternal UPD (~25%), imprinting defect. Angelman = loss of maternal UBE3A: maternal deletion (~70%), paternal UPD, UBE3A mutation, imprinting defect. DNA methylation analysis is the best first test for both
Beckwith–Wiedemann (11p15 imprinting): macrosomia, macroglossia, omphalocele, hemihypertrophy, neonatal hypoglycaemia, Wilms tumour and hepatoblastoma risk

**Lyon hypothesis**: random inactivation of one X in each female somatic cell early in embryogenesis (XIST); inactive X = Barr body; number of Barr bodies = number of X − 1. Skewed inactivation → manifesting female carriers (e.g. DMD, haemophilia). G6PD isoenzyme mosaicism proved clonality of tumours
Genetic anticipation is due to expansion during meiosis; repeat size correlates with earlier onset and severity
Robertsonian translocation (acrocentric 13, 14, 15, 21, 22) underlies ~4% of Down syndrome; a balanced 21;21 carrier parent cannot have a normal child

traps.stem: Child with suspected Prader–Willi; FISH for 15q11–q13 deletion is normal.
traps.trap: Excluding Prader–Willi syndrome.
traps.fix: FISH misses maternal UPD (~25%) and imprinting defects. DNA methylation analysis detects all three mechanisms and is the preferred first test.

traps.stem: A balanced reciprocal translocation is suspected in a couple with recurrent miscarriages. Which test?
traps.trap: Chromosomal microarray because it has higher resolution.
traps.fix: Microarray detects copy-number changes only and misses balanced rearrangements. Use conventional G-banded karyotype of both parents.

traps.stem: Neurological disease with anticipation transmitted through the mother in a congenital severe form.
traps.trap: Huntington disease, the classic anticipation example.
traps.fix: Huntington anticipation is via paternal transmission. Maternal transmission with congenital form = myotonic dystrophy type 1 (CTG); fragile X expansion also occurs in maternal meiosis.

cards.text: Prader–Willi results from loss of {{c1::paternal}} 15q11–q13 genes; Angelman from loss of maternal {{c2::UBE3A}}.
Fragile X: {{c1::CGG}} repeat in {{c2::FMR1}}; full mutation >200 repeats causes hypermethylation and silencing.

cards.front: Which test for: balanced translocation, 22q11 microdeletion, unexplained developmental delay?
cards.back:
Balanced translocation: karyotype.
22q11: FISH (or microarray).
Developmental delay / autism / multiple anomalies: chromosomal microarray (first-tier).

cards.text: Mitochondrial disorders are transmitted only {{c1::maternally}}; variable severity reflects {{c2::heteroplasmy}}.

cards.front: Lyon hypothesis in one line
cards.back: In each female somatic cell one X chromosome is randomly and permanently inactivated early in embryonic life (XIST), forming the Barr body; skewing explains manifesting carriers.
